Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

terrible adjective

very bad, awful

also awful, dreadful (very bad), horrible, terribly, a terrible journey, terrible weather, lousy, nasty

classical

Ter. Haut. 599: Pessima haec est meretrix.
Ter. Haut. 437: quia pessimē istōc in tē atque in illum cōnsulis

pessimus, pessima, pessimum

adjective, superlative of malus · Declension on Wiktionary

very bad, worst

As praise uses the superlative of bonus (see great), blame uses that of malus: “a terrible boy”, puer pessimus. The adverb is pessimē.

Other words

  • horribilis, horribile — awful, horrible

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 14.20.2: L. Antōnī horribilis cōntiō, Dolābellae praeclāra; Catull. 26.5: ō ventum horribilem atque pestilentem!; Traupman 154; Traupman 329 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Properly “frightful” (see terrible, causing fear); in Cicero’s letters and Catullus also the exaggeration of talk: an awful speech, a horrible wind.

  • foedus, foeda, foedum — foul, horrible (of weather, sights, smells)

    adjective · also used · classical · Liv. 29.18.5 (Lewis & Short): foedissima tempestās; Traupman 342 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Foul, ugly, loathsome; so of weather, a dreadful storm, and morally, shameful (Lewis & Short). A different word from foedus, foederis, a treaty.

  • incommodissimē — terribly badly, most uncomfortably

    adverb, superlative of incommodē · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 5.9.1: quī incommodissimē nāvigāssēmus · Wiktionary

    Of a journey or an arrangement that went badly (see comfortable).

  • dīrus, dīra, dīrum — dreadful, awful; properly ill-omened

    also used · classical · Lewis & Short; Traupman 275 · Declension on Wiktionary

Examples

  • Rōmae igitur dē Būthrōtō. L. Antōnī horribilis cōntiō, Dolābellae praeclāra.

    So we’ll deal with Buthrotum in Rome. Lucius Antonius made a terrible speech, Dolabella a splendid one.Cic. Att. 14.20.2

  • ō ventum horribilem atque pestilentem!

    oh, what a terrible, pestilent wind!Catull. 26.5

  • Actiō māluimus iter facere pedibus quī incommodissimē nāvigāssēmus

    after a terrible crossing, we preferred to go on from Actium on footCic. Att. 5.9.1

See also terrible, bad, great, wonderful.
